content:
One of the strangest features of modern life is that we live in a society that celebrates authenticity while quietly rewarding performance. We are constantly encouraged to be ourselves, to speak our truth, to bring our authentic selves to work, and to embrace individuality. Yet, in practice, many of the environments we inhabit reward something very different. They reward conformity, social awareness, and the ability to read a room whilst instinctively understanding what can and cannot be said. The result is that many people learn to present versions of themselves that fit the expectations of the moment, rather than revealing who they genuinely are.
I became fascinated by this long before I had the words to describe it. Over the years, I found myself increasingly noticing a gap between what people said publicly and what they appeared to believe privately. The more I paid attention, the more I realised this gap was not confined to politics, social media, or corporate life. It seemed to exist almost everywhere. That being said, my own awareness of it began through something much simpler, in that one of the most surprising things I learned was that people do not always say what they mean.
Growing up, communication was generally straightforward, if someone liked you, you knew it, if someone disliked you, you knew that too. If you were being foolish, someone would tell you. If you had put on weight, that observation would arrive with little warning and even less sensitivity. Relationships could be warm, arguments could be heated, and criticism could be uncomfortable, but there was usually very little ambiguity. You rarely had to wonder what people really thought because they tended to tell you.
Arriving in the UK felt like stepping into a different communication system altogether. People were polite, courteous, and often genuinely pleasant, yet I quickly realised there was another layer sitting beneath the surface. Many conversations seemed to operate on two levels simultaneously: the words being spoken and the meaning hidden underneath them. It took me a while to decode it, for example, “you look well” did not always mean you looked well, “that’s an interesting idea” was not always a compliment, “we should definitely do this again sometime” often had no intention attached to it whatsoever.
I found it confusing initially, then it became fascinating. Eventually, I began to wonder whether this tendency was confined to polite social interaction or whether it extended into something much deeper. The more I observed, the more I realised it was everywhere. I saw it in politics, in workplaces, in social circles, neighbourhoods, and professional networks. What I found the most intriguing was not dishonesty in the traditional sense, most of the people I encountered were not liars, they were not trying to deceive anyone. What fascinated me was something subtler, the performance.
Over time, I began noticing what I came to refer to as the social chameleons. These were people who seemed remarkably skilled at adapting themselves to whatever environment they occupied. They supported the right causes, used the right language, expressed the right views, and instinctively avoided the wrong ones. They were often intelligent, successful, well-liked, and socially aware. In many respects, they embodied exactly the kind of people modern society tends to reward.
Yet I often found myself asking the same question, how much of what I was seeing was genuine? And how much of it was survival? The question became increasingly difficult to ignore because I kept encountering situations where public behaviour and private beliefs did not seem to align. I would hear enthusiastic support for certain causes in meetings, only to hear entirely different opinions expressed in quieter settings. I would see people champion values publicly that they appeared to have little interest in practising privately. I would meet individuals who seemed passionate about inclusion, diversity, and social cohesion, yet whose actual lives remained remarkably insulated from people who were different from them.
What became clear was that many people were not necessarily expressing what they believed, they were expressing what was safe. This was particularly noticeable in the workplace. Modern organisations often encourage employees to bring their authentic selves to work. It is one of the most commonly repeated phrases in corporate culture. Yet many workplaces seem to reward the exact opposite. They reward conformity, they reward consensus and reward those who instinctively understand which opinions are safe to voice and which are best kept private.
The result is a culture where agreement is frequently mistaken for belief. People learn to support initiatives, language, and values not necessarily because they are convinced by them, but because opposing them carries social or professional risk. Over time, organisations begin confusing compliance with commitment and support becomes difficult to distinguish from performance. Most of this is not malicious, in fact, I believe much of it is entirely understandable. Humans naturally want to belong, want acceptance, opportunities, and to be liked. They want to avoid conflict and to avoid becoming the person in the room who thinks differently, because there is comfort in aligning yourself with the prevailing culture and safety in saying what is expected.
The problem arises when those incentives become more important than sincerity, because when people consistently suppress what they actually think in favour of what they think they should say, something important is lost. Honest disagreement disappears and authentic feedback becomes harder to find. Leaders start believing they have support they do not really have. Organisations convince themselves they are aligned when in reality, they are simply unchallenged. At first everything would appear healthy, because nobody is arguing and nobody is objecting, everyone would seem engaged and appear supportive, but beneath the surface, genuine trust would begin to fade.
The irony is that the cultures which appear most harmonious are sometimes the least honest. The absence of disagreement can look like unity when, in essence, it may simply be evidence that people no longer feel comfortable expressing what they actually think. This matters because from my perspective, progress depends on honesty and if people cannot challenge ideas, bad ideas survive longer than they should. If people cannot disagree openly, decision-makers would lose access to valuable information. If people become performers rather than participants, organisations would slowly drift away from reality. This is why I increasingly believe authenticity is not merely a personal virtue but a social necessity.
A society built on authentic disagreement can still move towards truth because uncomfortable conversations remain possible. A society built on polite pretence eventually loses interest in finding out what is true because doing so might disrupt the performance. The greatest danger is not that people disagree with one another, after all democracies, workplaces, communities, and relationships have always survived disagreement. The greater danger is that people stop expressing what they genuinely believe altogether.
In the end, when performance becomes more important than conviction, people stop asking what is right and start asking what is safe. Appearances gradually replace principles and consensus becomes more important than honesty. The performance continues because everyone understands the script, even if fewer and fewer people believe it. Everything would appear perfectly normal until we one day realise that nobody quite knows where anyone really stands, perhaps the strangest consequence of all. In a society that talks endlessly about authenticity, authenticity itself has become one of the rarest things to find.
summary: Why authenticity has become one of the rarest qualities in modern life—and how the pressure to perform conformity undermines genuine trust in workplaces and society.
title: The Age of Pretence

content:
As a black person, recent conversations about DEI has brought into focus concerns I’ve held about DEI and how I believe it is often used as marketing or PR material by institutions.
I’ve always observed that organisations, institutions, and society at large are normally keener to align to, or promote people with the humble, underdog narratives. For example, within the workplace, you often see employees handed the employee of the month awards not necessarily based on how well they’ve performed in their job, but because they were compassionate, kind to another colleague or were heroic. Undoubtedly admirable acts, but in most cases, totally unconnected to their job performance. Or television competitions like ‘X-Factor’ or ‘Britian’s got talent’, which to me normally seems to reward contestants with sob-stories over those with talent but no ‘story’, perhaps this is motivated by the producers’ perception of the appetite of its audience.
This societal propensity of wanting to back the underdog is what I believe drives these white saviour behaviours when it comes to DEI in organisations. Which is why I believe that often organisations and institutions treat DEI as a PR exercise and as a marketing opportunity to display how well they are doing when it comes to DEI, by prioritising the marketing narrative ahead of merit.
As long as our wider society yearns to hear the rags to riches and underdog story, organisations and institutions will continue to feed this need by exploiting DEI candidates for their marketing collateral, whilst seeking a pat on the back for their self-benefiting efforts.
I think the biggest problem is that this approach undermines the very spirit of DEI. Opportunities risk being skewed towards those with marketable stories, while equally talented people without a compelling “overcoming adversity” narrative are overlooked. Diversity should not depend on how inspirational someone appears to others.
What jars for me personally is the associated celebration of what should be unremarkable. A genuinely successful DEI culture is not one that constantly showcases itself, it is one where inclusion is so well embedded that nobody feels the need to applaud it. Real inclusion in my opinion shouldn’t be a headline, a campaign, or a photo opportunity, it should be the norm.
summary: A personal reflection on how organisations often treat DEI as a PR exercise—prioritising marketable underdog narratives over genuine inclusion and merit.
title: DEI as Marketing or PR Collateral Rather Than Merit Based

content:
I can’t quite remember the exact article that triggered it for me, not even the headline, nor the topic, or why I was even reading it. However, what I vividly remember is reading the comments section afterwards and saying something out loud that surprised even me, “Damn, I think critical thinking is dead.”
At the time, I dismissed it purely as a moment of frustration as opposed to an epiphany of some sort. After all, people arguing about politics, religion, sport, and current affairs was normal and prevalent. But despite my acknowledgement of this, the thought stayed with me ever since. And once it had been planted, I started noticing the same pattern all over the place.
At first, I saw it in online debates, the majority of people seemed to lack interest in understanding the person they disagreed with. They didn’t seem to be motivated by curiosity but were rather more concerned with victory. It felt like every issue had already been divided neatly into camps, and most people appeared to arrive at conversations with their position fully formed before the discussion had even commenced. The ‘debate’ itself felt performative considering the respective positions were predetermined and sometimes seemed immovable. The more I paid attention, the more I found it apparent and difficult ignore.
I saw it in politics, where I noticed supporters often defended parties and personalities with the same unwavering loyalty that football fans reserve for their clubs. I saw it in social issues, where complex topics were increasingly reduced to simplistic choices between two opposing sides. There was very little room for uncertainty, nuance, or the possibility that both sides might possess pieces of the truth. Ultimately you were deemed to be either for something or against it.
I wasn’t concerned about disagreement itself, in fact, quite the opposite as I believe that disagreement can be healthy. The problem was that fewer and fewer people seemed willing to evaluate their own assumptions. It increasingly felt as if people inherited opinions rather than arrived at them. They adopted beliefs from political tribes, friendship groups, news outlets, online communities, and professional networks. Then they defended those beliefs with remarkable confidence, often without ever questioning them seriously. This baffled me because I had always believed that changing your mind was a sign of growth, particularly in an intellectually developed society.
Many of the most important lessons in my own life came from discovering that something I previously believed was incomplete, naive, or simply wrong. There are too many examples to count, but I certainly recognise that moving to the UK challenged assumptions I did not even realise I held. In a similar vein, working in sustainability challenged others, then becoming older, becoming a parent, and navigating different social and professional environments added further layers of complexity. If learning is supposed to expand understanding, then surely it should occasionally disrupt certainty? Yet, modern discourse increasingly treats certainty as a virtue and the person who expresses doubt is perceived as being weak. I know first-hand that the person who asks awkward questions risks being viewed as difficult. The person who changes their position can often be accused of inconsistency. Meanwhile, the person who repeats the same view with complete confidence often receives admiration, even when that confidence is unsupported by evidence.
Social media has undoubtedly accelerated this trend. Perhaps because algorithms reward certainty because it is proportional to the engagement it generates. Strong opinions travel further than nuanced ones and outrage certainly spreads faster than reflection. Complex arguments struggle to compete with simplified narratives that fit neatly into a headline or a thirty-second video. As a result, people are bombarded with information while becoming increasingly vulnerable to intellectual shortcuts. Despite the fact that we know more than any generation in history, I sometimes wonder whether we are spending less time thinking about what we know. The irony is that access to this level of information has so much potential. However, it seems it has often encouraged us to delegate our thinking to whichever tribe, commentator, influencer, or political camp we already agree with.
I see this tendency everywhere. At work, where people often instinctively align themselves with prevailing opinions because challenging consensus can be uncomfortable. In politics, where people defend policies they would have criticised had they been proposed by the opposing party. In social debates, where belonging to the correct side often appears more important than understanding the issue itself. And, perhaps most surprisingly, I see it in the sustainability sector I work in.
This may sound strange because sustainability is often portrayed as a rational, evidence-led discipline. Yet, in reality, sustainability operates within a world of competing priorities, imperfect information, and difficult trade-offs. Making real progress often requires balancing environmental concerns, social needs, economic realities, political constraints, and human behaviour. Nothing about balancing that complex equation is simple. Yet in my professional life, I have frequently encountered pressure to fully embrace particular narratives or reject them entirely. Certain discussions sometimes feel as though they have already been settled before they have properly been examined. I’ve found that questioning assumptions can be interpreted as opposition rather than curiosity. This should concern all of us because critical thinking is not the enemy of progress, it is actually one of the conditions that enables progress. Without it, we become emotionally attached to ideas that may not be delivering the outcomes we want. We continue supporting approaches because they sound right, feel right, or align with our identity rather than because they are actually the best option.
To be clear, I don’t believe the purpose of critical thinking is to reject popular ideas simply because they are popular, nor be to be sceptical or contrarian for the sake of it. Rather, I think that critical thinking is fundamentally an act of humility, because it requires us to create enough distance between ourselves and our beliefs to examine them honestly. Asking the challenging questions; Why do I think this? How do I know it is true? What evidence would change my mind? Could I be wrong? Those questions are uncomfortable precisely because they challenge certainty, but they are also the questions that drive learning.
Every meaningful advance in human history began with someone willing to question what everybody else accepted. Scientific breakthroughs, social reforms, technological innovations, and cultural shifts all emerged because individuals were prepared to challenge prevailing assumptions. We need to recognise that the common thread was not intelligence, it was curiosity and a willingness to risk being wrong in pursuit of a better understanding.
That is why I find the current state of public discourse so troubling, not because people disagree more, but because fewer people seem interested in discovering whether their position is in fact correct. As the objective increasingly appears to be defending belief rather than pursuing truth. Perhaps that is why that offhand comment, to myself, several years ago has continued to resonate with me. Critical thinking is dead. I do not literally believe it is dead, of course, but I do believe it is under pressure.
I believe we are living in an age of unprecedented access to knowledge, while simultaneously losing some of the habits required to interpret it wisely and objectively. The challenge facing modern society is not a shortage of information, but finding enough curiosity, humility, and intellectual courage to question what we think we already know. Because a society that stops asking questions may continue accumulating knowledge, but it will gradually lose the ability to understand it.
summary: Why modern society increasingly rewards certainty over curiosity—and how intellectual shortcuts undermine genuine inquiry, even iacross_column.pngn evidence-led sectors like sustainability.
title: Critical Thinking is Dead

Welcome I am Kuram Gwakyaa, an award-winning sustainability leader, writer and public speaker. My writing explores sustainability, culture, identity, social behaviour, and the gap between what societies claim to value and how they actually behave.
I believe sustainability is not about distant ambitions or corporate commitments alone. It is about empowering people, influencing behaviour, and delivering measurable action where it matters most.
As an award-winning sustainability leader, Chartered Environmentalist, author, and founder of Sustainability Loft, I have spent more than fifteen years helping organisations transform sustainability from a strategic aspiration into an operational reality. My work combines sustainability, social value, compliance, quality, and organisational transformation to create solutions that deliver lasting environmental, social, and business outcomes.
Through thought leadership, public speaking, writing, and community engagement, I am committed to making sustainability understandable, achievable, and relevant to everyone. Adapted from the IFE Career Insights Series
Introduction Hi, I’m Kuram Gwakyaa. I am a consultant here at Kulexar Consulting Limited. I am also an Associate Member of the Institution of Fire Engineers (IFE) and hold interim Chartered Engineer status with them.
When people ask how I arrived at this point in my career, I always tell them that my journey into the fire sector was not a linear one by any chance. It was a path built on curiosity, taking on challenges, and constantly adapting to new environments.
A Non-Linear Journey: From Auditing to Passive Fire Protection My entry into the fire industry started in a role where I served as a QSHE (Quality, Safety, Health, and Environment) Advisor. That position in itself involved a substantial amount of auditing to various standards and spearheading a wide variety of fire-related initiatives.
Through my work on those initiatives, I was led into a new role that focused specifically on third-party certification auditing. This role was a turning point for me, as it covered passive fire protection. From then on, I have never looked back.
Along the way, I have gained a wealth of relevant experience, specialized expertise, and industry qualifications. Each step of this non-linear path has built upon the last, ultimately leading me to my current consulting role within the fire sector.
A Day in the Life of a Fire Consultant In my current consulting position, the work is incredibly diverse. On any given day, my responsibilities involve:
Carrying out comprehensive risk assessments to identify potential hazards; Conducting meticulous audit preparations to ensure compliance with standards; Performing detailed compartmentation surveys to evaluate how fire can be contained within a building; and Providing vital passive fire protection advice to our clients. What I enjoy most about this role is the profound sense that I am truly making a difference. I am supporting the effort to make buildings safer, and ultimately, as we all say in the fire industry, the end goal is all about protecting life. Having that direct hand in protecting people gives me an immense sense of pride in my daily work.
Furthermore, fire consulting is a highly dynamic area to work in. It offers a tremendous amount of variety in everything you do—no two days are quite the same. It also grants you the privilege of meeting and working with people from a wide range of different backgrounds in all your professional endeavors.
Advice for Aspiring and Early-Career Professionals For anyone trying to enter the fire industry, or for those who are still early in their careers within the fire sector, I would offer these key pieces of advice:
“Never be afraid to challenge yourself. Keep the challenge there—that in itself will lead you places.”
Follow your interests: Let your genuine curiosity guide your career steps. Stay motivated to learn: Continuous learning is one aspect of this sector that you simply cannot do without. Regulations and technologies are constantly evolving—they keep changing almost every day. If you are able to keep up with your learning in that regard, it will go a very long way in your professional development. Keep an open mind: Staying open to new ideas, different perspectives, and unexpected roles is the key to getting the absolute best out of your career. The Value of IFE Membership Gaining membership with the Institution of Fire Engineers (IFE) was an incredibly important milestone for me.
Firstly, it offered me that essential professional credibility that most practitioners in our industry seek, especially considering the high status and reputation of the IFE.
Secondly, it has provided me with reliable, high-quality knowledge resources that I can always tap into whenever I need support or guidance.
Finally, there is a powerful networking angle. When I attend IFE events, I am able to network, share ideas, and connect with a large community of peers across the industry. It is an invaluable community that keeps us all connected and moving forward.
summary: Why the most impactful careers are rarely linear and how transitioning skillsets highlights the vital connection between professional credibility and lifelong curiosity.
title: ECNG Career Insight Series: My Journey into Fire Consulting and the Power of Continuous Learning

This article is based on Kuram Gwakyaa’s keynote presentation at Sustainability LIVE.
Executive Summary Facilities management (FM) sits at the critical boundary where strategic climate ambitions meet daily operational reality. In this talk, Kuram Gwakyaa, Head of Sustainability at Mitie, shares insights on how FM can evolve from a conventional maintenance function into a core driver of net-zero transformation and organizational resilience.
Key Highlights & Core Insights 1. From Ambition to Execution While setting corporate targets is essential, decarbonisation is won or lost in execution. Facilities management controls crucial levers across energy efficiency, building operations, waste reduction, and occupant engagement. Moving from ambition to on-the-ground reality requires:
Baseline Accuracy: Leveraging smart metering and building diagnostics to establish precise baseline metrics. Phased Retrofitting: Upgrading building infrastructure—such as heat pumps, LED systems, and renewable generation—aligned with building lifecycle windows. Operational Efficiency: Continuous tuning of Building Management Systems (BMS) to eliminate off-peak energy waste. 2. FM as a Strategic Lever With the built environment accounting for approximately 40% of global greenhouse gas emissions, facilities managers hold the keys to immediate Scope 1 and Scope 2 emission reductions. By embedding sustainability criteria directly into standard operating procedures and procurement frameworks, FM teams deliver measurable environmental impact.
3. The Power of Integrated Engineering & Safety As clean technologies like Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and electric vehicle infrastructure are deployed at scale, sustainability efforts must incorporate rigorous engineering standards, fire safety protocols, and regulatory compliance (including ISO 50001 and ISO 14001).
Watch & Listen The full talk is available on-demand via Sustainability Magazine.
summary: In this keynote presentation for Sustainability LIVE, Kuram Gwakyaa explores how Facilities Management is at the forefront of the transition to a greener, more resilient future.
title: Sustainability LIVE: Leading the Transformation of Facilities Management for a Sustainable Future

content:
Ahead of Sustainability LIVE London, Kuram Gwakyaa, Head of Sustainability at Mitie (leading the Department for Work & Pensions account), shared key insights with Sustainability Magazine regarding workplace transformation, ESG reporting, and the emerging trends shaping the next decade.
What Inspires Your Involvement at Sustainability LIVE? “From previous experience attending Sustainability LIVE, I was inspired by the wealth of insights shared by keynote speakers and panellists. The event offers a valuable chance to engage with industry peers, fostering the exchange of ideas and best practices.”
Core Focus: Facilities Transformation In an era defined by climate urgency, digital transformation, and evolving workforce expectations, the workplace has become a strategic lever for driving sustainability, performance, and social impact.
At Mitie, Facilities Transformation represents a holistic approach that integrates:
Smart Technologies to monitor and optimize asset performance in real time. Environmental Stewardship to accelerate zero-carbon targets across major accounts. Community Value to ensure facility operations deliver lasting social benefit. 4 Emerging Trends Shaping the Next Decade of Sustainability Kuram highlighted four pivotal trends that will define the future of facilities management and the built environment:
1. Smart, Sustainable Infrastructure The convergence of AI, IoT sensors, and advanced data analytics is revolutionising facility management. Real-time data on energy use, space occupancy, and environmental conditions allows buildings to dynamically adjust operations, reducing emissions while optimizing occupant comfort. Tools like Mitie’s Emissions Intelligence provide real-time compliance and decarbonisation tracking.
2. ESG-Driven Compliance & Double Materiality With regulatory frameworks evolving rapidly—such as the UK Sustainability Disclosure Requirements (SDR) aligning with ISSB and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)—transparency is paramount. Organizations are shifting toward assessing double materiality: demonstrating both financial performance and broader environmental/social impact through traceable, audit-ready supply chains.
3. Circular Economy & Responsible Resource Use Rethinking procurement, asset maintenance, and end-of-life strategies is essential for circularity. In facilities management, this means repurposing furniture, refurbishing HVAC systems, responsible sourcing, and eliminating single-use waste streams throughout property operations.
4. Social Value and DEI Integration Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) is no longer separate from ESG strategy—it is a core business resilience imperative. Embedding inclusive hiring, employee wellbeing, and local community engagement into facility operations ensures that sustainability efforts generate tangible social value alongside carbon reduction.
Key Takeaway “The next decade will redefine what it means to deliver high-performing places. It’s no longer just about operational efficiency; it’s about creating spaces that are sustainable, inclusive, and future-ready.”
Original Article Read the full feature on Sustainability Magazine.
summary: Ahead of Sustainability LIVE London, Kuram Gwakyaa sat down with Sustainability Magazine to discuss Facilities Transformation, four emerging sustainability trends for the next decade, and driving ESG impact.
title: Sustainability LIVE Q&A: Redefining Workplaces, Smart Infrastructure, and ESG Leadership

content:
Ahead of Sustainability LIVE: Net Zero at the QEII Centre, Kuram Gwakyaa, Head of Sustainability at Mitie Group, spoke with Sustainability Magazine about the upcoming Global ESG Strategies panel, navigating emerging regulatory frameworks, and why integrating DEI into sustainability is vital for long-term business resilience.
Context: Sustainability LIVE: Net Zero 2025 Held at London’s QEII Centre on 5–6 March 2025, Sustainability LIVE: Net Zero brings together sustainability leaders, investors, and supply chain specialists to explore practical pathways toward a carbon-neutral future.
Co-located with Procurement & Supply Chain LIVE: Sustainability, the summit addresses key drivers of the global net-zero agenda—from ESG reporting mandates and carbon pricing mechanisms to low-carbon logistics and circular economy models.
At the summit, Kuram Gwakyaa joins the ‘Global ESG Strategies’ panel alongside:
Joe Murphy, Executive Lead, Ellen MacArthur Foundation Michael Batstone, Global Climate Strategy Manager, IFS Olivia Ruggles-Brise, Vice President for Sustainability, BCD Travel What Inspired Your Involvement in Sustainability LIVE: Net Zero? “Having previously attended Sustainability LIVE, I found that the event presented attendees with an array of adaptable ideas and insights that emanated from the keynote speakers and panel discussions.
It also provided a valuable opportunity to network and connect with other industry peers, which is particularly beneficial in terms of sharing experience and best practices. As a result, I felt inspired to get involved because it is the right platform for sharing ideas and broadly raising awareness for Sustainability.”
(Note: Mitie was recognized at the Global Sustainability & ESG Awards 2024, taking home the Diversity Award for its dedication to driving equity and inclusion across operations.)
Global ESG Strategies: What Will the Panel Focus On? With ESG performance increasingly tied to commercial success for industry leaders like Mitie, the panel explores how organizations transition from high-level commitments to operational reality.
“With the increasing importance of ESG considerations for top-performing organisations like Mitie, my panel discussion will focus on providing attendees with insights into the development and implementation of global ESG strategies.
The discussion will revolve around operationally embedding and integrating ESG principles, taking into account regulations, supply chain considerations, innovation and sustainable growth.”
Key Objectives for the Event Kuram outlined three primary goals for participating in Sustainability LIVE: Net Zero:
Engage with Cross-Sector Leaders: Connecting with peers across industries to align on shared decarbonisation hurdles. Exchange Adaptable Ideas: Gaining actionable insights and operational methodologies that can be implemented on major accounts. Advance Industry Knowledge: Contributing to the broader discourse and raising awareness through active panel dialogue. Emerging Trends Shaping the Next Decade of Sustainability Reflecting on recent developments—including the UK SDR aligning with ISSB and the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)—Kuram outlined key areas set to define sustainability over the next decade:
1. Responsible Sourcing & Full Value-Chain Visibility Supply chain scrutiny is intensifying. Organizations must understand their full end-to-end value chain, leveraging technologies such as blockchain for traceability and adopting near-shoring strategies to mitigate geopolitical risk while curbing freight emissions.
2. Corporate Transparency & Double Materiality The era of surface-level reporting is over. Scrutiny-proof strategies now demand double materiality assessments, where companies evaluate both the financial materiality of climate risks to their business and the outward environmental and social impact of their operations.
3. Green Finance & Nature-Based Solutions Financial instruments are pivoting toward environmental restoration. Following pivotal discussions at COP16 and COP29, green finance will play a decisive role in funding biodiversity initiatives and nature-based solutions alongside traditional carbon reduction.
4. Navigating the Energy Transition While global investment in renewables now outpaces fossil fuels, the transition faces mounting complexity due to shifting geopolitical dynamics, grid capacity bottlenecks, and volatile market forces.
Deep Dive: DEI Integration as a Driver of Business Resilience Among these trends, Kuram emphasized that the integration of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) into ESG strategies is one of the most critical evolutions for modern enterprises.
“From my perspective, the growing focus on DEI and its integration within ESG strategies is the trend to watch in terms of embedding ESG within business operations as well as contributing to business resilience.
This is particularly pertinent, given that organisations are recognising that the role of ESG has shifted from a ‘nice to have’, to a strategic ‘must-have’. ESG’s relevance to investment, talent attraction, retention and competitive advantage has become clear. One key element of this trend is the focus on people, captured within the Social Value aspect that encompasses DEI.”
Why DEI is Essential to Commercial Success Tender & Contract Requirements: In sectors like facilities management, Social Value and robust DEI commitments are increasingly mandatory within public and private procurement criteria. Having a demonstrable DEI framework is decisive in winning new business. Attracting and Retaining Top Talent: Modern professionals increasingly select employers based on workplace culture, wellbeing, and inclusive environments. The Multi-Generational Workplace: Citing research from Ernst & Young (EY), Kuram highlighted that for the first time, five distinct generations (Boomers, Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z, and Gen Alpha) are collaborating in the workplace. Managing this diversity requires proactive leadership focused on continuous upskilling and AI-driven engagement. Data-Driven Decision Making: Advances in AI and analytics provide real-time engagement data and benchmarking, enabling leadership teams to make responsive, measurable decisions across their workforce. “Although there are understandable complexities associated with DEI integration, it is an area that would gather momentum and has the potential to support a meaningful and impactful ESG transformation in the next decade.”

summary: Ahead of Sustainability LIVE: Net Zero at the QEII Centre, Kuram Gwakyaa sat down with Sustainability Magazine to discuss global ESG strategies, corporate transparency, and embedding DEI into business resilience.
